extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and American history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical analysis of early American journalism focusing on the Alien and Sedition Acts, press politics, and editorial practice around the turn of the 19th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien Act (1798)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alien act ... permitted the President to order out of the country all such aliens as he should deem 'dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States.' Any alien who was found in the country after receiving such an order was liable to imprisonment for three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized in the text as 'without parallel in American legislation.' Presented as a legal instrument that could be and was used against immigrant editors and political opponents (e.g., actions against those suspected of stirring sedition). Illustration: government agents used these powers in prosecutions and to intimidate the foreign-born press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition Act (July 14, 1798)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sedition act ... made it a high misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of $5,000 and five years' imprisonment, for persons to unlawfully combine or conspire against the government, or to write, print, publish or quote any false scandal or scurrilous writings against the government of the United States, the President or either House of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates the criminalized conduct and penalties and is shown in the chapter as the principal legal tool used to prosecute editors and printers. Examples and consequences: numerous indictments and convictions of Republican editors; trials carried out under judges and marshals sympathetic to the administration. Anti-pattern: use of the law to suppress legitimate political criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a defense in libel (amendment by Bayard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment ... permitting the truth of the matter contained in the publication to be given in evidence as a good defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a 'revolutionary' change in law, but initially accepted in only two states; the text notes that it was not until later defenses (e.g., Alexander Hamilton's defense of Croswell) and subsequent state enactments that truth became widely accepted as a libel defense. Practical implication for journalists: truthful reporting could, in principle, be used to resist libel prosecutions, but reliance on this protection was uncertain in 1798–1804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan (biased) jury selection in Sedition prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The juries summoned by the marshal were all Federalists, and only Federalists were selected to try those who were indicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a procedural anti-pattern that undermined fair trials and magnified the political effect of the Sedition prosecutions. Examples: trials of Republican editors where juries were packed with Federalists, contributing to convictions and political suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of press content: coarseness and scurrility
rubrics_metrics.description: The press tended toward coarseness and sometimes indecency ... no one then writing could compare with Cobbett in either bitterness or vulgarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the narrative to explain why the Federalists felt justified in attacking the press, but the text cautions that coarseness was not unique to one party. Evaluative implication: while coarse and scurrilous content existed, it did not, by itself, legitimize legal suppression; historians should not treat vulgarity as a sole justification for censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as political actor / the Fourth Estate
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper press ... distinct assumption of political functions by the newspaper press ... the will of the people was expressed through the newspaper press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames a normative criterion for assessing journalism's role: newspapers were active political agents shaping popular will and policy. This explains both the power of the press and the anxiety of political elites; useful when evaluating historical influence of newspapers and editorial responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government patronage and printing as influence on editorial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sought government printing and other patronage (e.g., Duane opened a store hoping to obtain the government printing; Jefferson promised to help him purchase supplies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how access to government printing contracts and appointments (postmasterships, etc.) could shape editors' behavior and loyalties. As a criterion: watch for financial or patronage ties that may bias editorial content; anti-patterns include pursuing office or contracts in exchange for favorable coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial partisanship / the party press model
rubrics_metrics.description: Many editors acted as party writers; newspapers (e.g., the Aurora, Argus, Evening Post) were vigorously partisan and engaged in personal and political attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter treats partisanship as the dominant model of the era's press — an explanatory criterion when judging content and motives. Consequences include ferocious political warfare, prosecutions under sedition laws, and duels; modern assessment should account for the normative acceptability of partisan journalism in the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial authorship practices (statesman‑dictated content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton ... was in the habit of seeing Coleman ... to dictate and I to note down in shorthand; when he stops, my article is completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a production practice where political leaders directly shaped newspaper text. As a criterion for provenance and responsibility: articles may reflect the views of powerful patrons rather than the nominal editor; raises issues of transparency and authorship attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct norms: dueling and personal violence among editors
rubrics_metrics.description: A continual exchange of personalities ... Several duels resulted ... Thompson was mortally wounded ... The editor of the Evening Post was at his office the next day as if nothing had occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents contemporaneous norms of honor that intersected with journalism. For evaluating historical journalism culture: consider that personal honor codes (including dueling) influenced conflicts and the tenor of editorial rivalry; by modern standards this is an anti-pattern in professional conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leadership must read public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: These famous laws grew out of the failure of Adams and other Federalists to properly understand public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poses a criterion for evaluating political decision-making connected to press policy: successful leaders should gauge public opinion; failure to do so can produce unpopular, repressive legislation that backfires politically (as it did for the Federalists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutionality dispute / states' right to judge federal acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginia passed resolutions denying their constitutionality, and sent copies ... Massachusetts ... passed a resolution upholding the laws and condemning the Virginia resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames an important legal/political standard relevant to press-law disputes: whether states may judge constitutionality of federal acts. The press participated in and amplified this debate (e.g., newspapers protesting the denial of state decision-making). Relevant when assessing editorial positioning on constitutional questions.
